---
title: "Fear Gauges and Headlines"
subtitle: "Testing a correlation two ways: across time, and across countries"
---

<span class="kicker">Machine Learning for Social Science &nbsp;·&nbsp; Boston, MA</span>

::: {.lead}
Two series can move together for a good reason, or for no reason at all &mdash; ice
cream sales and crime rates both rise in summer, but neither causes the other; a
warmer season drives both. This post works through two correlations that hold up
better, testing each two different ways: once over time within a single place, and
once across places at a single point in time.
:::

## Example 1: Market fear and the news, over time

**The variables.** The **CBOE Volatility Index (VIX)** is the options market's
30-day forward-looking measure of expected S&P 500 volatility &mdash; Wall Street's
"fear gauge." The **San Francisco Fed Daily News Sentiment Index** is a daily
sentiment score built by scoring economics-related articles across 16 major U.S.
newspapers, smoothed into a continuous time series back to 1980. Both are daily,
both are United States&ndash;based, and both are free to download.

**Sourcing.** VIX: CBOE Volatility Index, retrieved from FRED (Federal Reserve Bank
of St. Louis), series `VIXCLS`. News sentiment: Shapiro, Sudhof & Wilson (2020),
*Daily News Sentiment Index*, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. The overlap
between the two series runs from **January 3, 2000 to September 11, 2026** &mdash;
6,747 trading days.

### Descriptive statistics

<div class="stat-card">
<div class="lbl">VIX &middot; mean</div>
<div class="val">19.79</div>
<div class="note">sd 8.27 &middot; range 9.14&ndash;82.69</div>
</div>
<div class="stat-card">

<div class="note">right-skewed, as fear gauges tend to be</div>
</div>

</div>

</div>
</div>

### The chart

Monthly averages of both series, January 2000&ndash;September 2026:

<div style="position:relative; height:380px; margin: 1.5rem 0;">
<canvas id="vixSentChart"></canvas>
</div>

### Correlation

<div class="stat-grid">
<div class="stat-card">
<div class="lbl">Pearson r &middot; levels</div>
<div class="val">&minus;0.61</div>
<div class="note">p &lt; 0.001, n = 6,747 daily obs.</div>
</div>
<div class="stat-card">
<div class="lbl">Pearson r &middot; daily changes</div>
<div class="val pos">0.005</div>
<div class="note">p = 0.66 &mdash; not distinguishable from zero</div>
</div>
</div>

The **levels** of VIX and news sentiment are strongly negatively correlated
(r = &minus;0.61): when the market is fearful, the news is gloomier, and vice versa.
That is the correlation most people mean when they say "the market and the news
move together." But when the same two series are converted to **day-over-day
changes** &mdash; did VIX and sentiment move together *from one day to the next*
&mdash; the correlation collapses to essentially zero. That gap is itself the
lesson: a strong correlation in levels can come almost entirely from both series
drifting through the same multi-year regimes (calm 2000s, the 2008 crisis, COVID,
etc.), not from any tight day-to-day linkage between newsroom tone and options
pricing.

## Example 2: Policy uncertainty and market volatility, across countries

**The variables.** **Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU)**, the Baker-Bloom-Davis
index built from the frequency of policy-uncertainty language in national
newspapers, one score per country per month. Paired against each country's
**equity volatility** for the same month &mdash; the VIX-style implied-volatility
reading where a clean monthly figure was obtainable.

**Sourcing.** EPU: `policyuncertainty.com`, "All Country Data." Volatility: VIX
monthly average from FRED (`VIXCLS`); German DAX implied volatility from Eurex's
official *VSTOXX Derivatives: July 2026 Recap*; India VIX from NSE-sourced daily
market reports (HDFC Sky), averaged across the month's available sessions; S&amp;P/ASX
200 VIX monthly average from ASX's own *Group Monthly Activity Report, July 2026*.
The month is **July 2026**.[^countries]

[^countries]: A cross-country volatility comparison was originally planned across
eight markets &mdash; the United States, the Eurozone, Germany, the United Kingdom,
Japan, India, South Korea, and Australia &mdash; using each market's own
implied-volatility index (VIX, VSTOXX, VDAX, VFTSE, Nikkei VI, India VIX, VKOSPI,
and the S&amp;P/ASX 200 VIX). Reliable, verifiable monthly figures could only be
sourced for four of these (United States, Germany, India, Australia); the other
four are left out here rather than estimated from incomplete data. South Korea in
particular saw VKOSPI spike to record levels in July 2026 amid an acute
geopolitical shock, which would have made it a genuine outlier had a reliable
monthly figure been available.

### Descriptive statistics, July 2026

| Country | EPU index | Equity volatility |
|---|---:|---:|
| United States | 219.3 | 17.09 |
| Germany | 720.6 | 13.77 |
| India | 152.4 | 12.83 |
| Australia | 183.0 | 11.30 |

<div class="val">318.8</div>
<div class="note">sd 265.8 &middot; Germany is the high outlier</div>
</div>
<div class="stat-card">
<div class="lbl">Volatility &middot; mean (n=4)</div>
<div class="val">13.75</div>
<div class="note">sd 2.43 &middot; a tight, unremarkable range</div>
</div>
</div>

### The chart

<div style="position:relative; height:380px; margin: 1.5rem 0;">
<canvas id="epuVolChart"></canvas>
</div>

### Correlation

<div class="stat-grid">
<div class="stat-card">
<div class="lbl">Pearson r</div>
<div class="val pos">0.08</div>
<div class="note">p = 0.92, n = 4 countries</div>
</div>
<div class="stat-card">
<div class="lbl">Spearman &rho;</div>
<div class="val pos">0.60</div>
<div class="note">p = 0.40 &mdash; a moderate rank relationship, not significant</div>
</div>
</div>

With only four countries, this correlation carries almost no statistical weight on
its own (n = 4 leaves just two degrees of freedom) &mdash; it is included to show
the *mechanics* of a cross-sectional correlation, not to make a claim about the
world. Worth noticing anyway: Germany has by far the highest EPU reading (roughly
three times the next-highest country) but a middling volatility reading, which
alone is enough to flatten the linear (Pearson) relationship even though the rank
(Spearman) relationship still points positive.

## Why the correlation might not mean what it looks like

**In the time-series example**, the headline result (r = &minus;0.61 in levels, r
&asymp; 0 in changes) points to a specific third factor: the **macroeconomic
regime**. VIX and news sentiment both drift with the business cycle &mdash; both
were low and calm for most of the mid-2000s, both moved sharply in 2008 and again
in 2020 &mdash; so a big share of their correlation in *levels* is really both
series independently tracking the same underlying economic conditions, rather than
one driving the other day to day. The fact that the correlation nearly disappears
in first differences is the tell.

**In the cross-country example**, the plausible third factor is different: EPU
counts *newspaper mentions* of policy uncertainty, while an implied-volatility
index prices *option-market risk*. A country can generate a great deal of
uncertainty-flavored news coverage &mdash; coalition politics, fiscal debates,
regulatory fights &mdash; without that translating into elevated pricing of equity
risk, and Germany in July 2026 looks like exactly that case. The two variables are
related in principle (both are trying to measure "uncertainty") but are constructed
from different underlying processes (text mentions vs. option prices), which is
enough to decouple them country by country.

          ticks: { color: '#94a3b8' },
          grid: { color: '#1e2d45' }
        },
        y: {
          title: { display: true, text: 'Equity volatility (implied, %)', color: '#94a3b8' },
          ticks: { color: '#94a3b8' },
          grid: { color: '#1e2d45' }
        }
      },
      plugins: {
        legend: { display: false },
        tooltip: {
          callbacks: {
            label: function(ctx) {
              const d = ctx.raw;
              return `${d.country}: EPU ${d.x}, vol ${d.y}`;
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  });
})();
</script>
